explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The leaders say the people of Israel “…have not kept themselves separate from the surrounding peoples…” (Ezra 9:1). They say it reaches the priests and Levites too. That's the whole complaint, right there in the first verse.

Nobody in this report is checking a bank balance. The leaders never mention a debt or a bill. Their complaint is that the people haven't kept themselves separate from the surrounding peoples. That's the line to hold onto.

I get why a treaty sounds official, friend, but there's no signed paperwork in this report. The leaders say the people of Israel “…have not kept themselves separate from the surrounding peoples…” (Ezra 9:1). The problem is staying separate, not keeping a deal. Ezra is about to react to exactly that.

explanations.answer: They married women from those peoples
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The leaders say “…the Israelites have taken some of their daughters as wives for themselves and their sons, so that the holy seed has been mixed with the people of the land.” (Ezra 9:2). Marriage is how the report says the mixing happened. The leaders put it that plainly.

explanations.answer: They traded in those peoples' markets
explanations.explanation: Markets would be a nice, calm answer, friend, but the report doesn't mention them. No stalls, no haggling, no shopping bags. The leaders say the Israelites took some of those peoples' daughters as wives for themselves and their sons (Ezra 9:2). That's how the mixing happened.

explanations.answer: They served in those peoples' armies
explanations.explanation: No armies in this report, baker. Nobody puts on a uniform. The leaders say the Israelites “…have taken some of their daughters as wives for themselves and their sons…” (Ezra 9:2). Marriage is the way they say it happened.

Not quite, friend. The report says the opposite. The leaders say “…the leaders and officials have taken the lead in this unfaithfulness!” (Ezra 9:2). So the leaders and officials were out front, not on the sidelines. The ones giving the report are naming their own.

False is right, baker. The report says “…the leaders and officials have taken the lead in this unfaithfulness!” (Ezra 9:2). They weren't standing back. They were out front. That makes it a hard report to deliver.

True, baker. Ezra says, “When I heard this report, I tore my tunic and cloak…” (Ezra 9:3). That's no polite "hmm, interesting." I think this one hit him in the gut. It's a heavy moment, so let's let it be heavy.

Ezra's reaction is a lot bigger than that, friend. He says, “When I heard this report, I tore my tunic and cloak…” (Ezra 9:3). He doesn't just nod and move along. He tears the clothes he's wearing, and there's more to come. It's a heavy moment.

explanations.answer: Everyone who trembled at God's words
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Ezra says “…everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gathered around me because of the unfaithfulness of the exiles…” (Ezra 9:4). They come to him, and they're not there for small talk. It's a quiet crowd, I bet.

Those officials show up earlier, friend. In Ezra 8:36 the king's edicts are delivered to the royal satraps and governors. Here, the text says it's everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel who gathers around Ezra (Ezra 9:4). Different crowd.

Artaxerxes, king of Persia (Ezra 7:1), has his officials somewhere else in this book, baker. They're not at this gathering. Ezra says the ones who gather around him are “…everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel…” (Ezra 9:4). It's the people who take God's words seriously.

explanations.answer: Kneels and spreads his hands to God
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Ezra says, “…I fell on my knees, spread out my hands to the LORD my God…” (Ezra 9:5). His first move is toward God. After that comes the prayer.
Ezra isn't calling a meeting yet, friend. The text says he fell on his knees and spread out his hands to the LORD his God (Ezra 9:5). No speeches, no planning session. He turns to God first.

explanations.answer: Writes a letter to the king
explanations.explanation: No letter in this scene, baker. Ezra says he “…fell on my knees, spread out my hands to the LORD my God…” (Ezra 9:5). No pen, no scroll, no waiting on a reply. He talks straight to God.

Right on, baker. Ezra prays, “…our iniquities are higher than our heads, and our guilt has reached the heavens.” (Ezra 9:6). It's stacked higher than he can reach, then higher than the sky. That's a man who isn't shrinking anything.

It's going the other way, friend. Ezra says their iniquities are “…higher than our heads…” and their guilt “…has reached the heavens.” (Ezra 9:6). Things that are shrinking don't pile up that high. He's describing something enormous.

Nothing's tucked away here, baker. Ezra is on his knees saying it out loud to God. He says their iniquities are “…higher than our heads, and our guilt has reached the heavens.” (Ezra 9:6). That's guilt out in the open and enormous.

That's the one, baker. Ezra says, “Because of our iniquities, we and our kings and priests have been delivered into the hands of the kings of the earth…” (Ezra 9:7). The sword, captivity, pillage and humiliation all come back to that. He says it about himself and his people, not about someone else.

explanations.answer: Because their walls were too weak
explanations.explanation: Walls are a natural guess, friend, but Ezra doesn't name them as the cause. He says, “Because of our iniquities, we and our kings and priests have been delivered into the hands of the kings of the earth…” (Ezra 9:7). He puts it on their iniquities, not on the stonework.

explanations.answer: Because their kings made no treaties
explanations.explanation: Treaties never come up in Ezra's list, baker. He says, “Because of our iniquities, we and our kings and priests have been delivered into the hands of the kings of the earth…” (Ezra 9:7). The reason he gives is their iniquities. That's the answer to hold onto.

explanations.answer: New life and light to their eyes
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Ezra says, “Even in our bondage, our God has given us new life and light to our eyes.” (Ezra 9:8). It's a bright line after a dark prayer. Notice he says it even in bondage.

explanations.answer: Herds and flocks in every field
explanations.explanation: Ezra doesn't mention a single animal, friend. He says, “Even in our bondage, our God has given us new life and light to our eyes.” (Ezra 9:8). What he's thankful for is life and light. Nothing about the fields.

explanations.answer: Grain and wine in their storehouses
explanations.explanation: A full storehouse would be a nice gift, baker, but Ezra doesn't list one. He says, “Even in our bondage, our God has given us new life and light to our eyes.” (Ezra 9:8). It's new life and light that he names.
Right, baker. Ezra says, “…He has extended to us grace in the sight of the kings of Persia…” (Ezra 9:9). He says it even while calling them slaves. He sees God's grace in the middle of that.

Egypt shows up in this chapter, friend, but only as one of the peoples in the leaders' list (Ezra 9:1). Ezra says God's grace was extended “…in the sight of the kings of Persia…” (Ezra 9:9). Different place, different kings.
Assyria doesn't come up anywhere in this prayer, baker. Ezra says God “…has extended to us grace in the sight of the kings of Persia…” (Ezra 9:9). Persia is the answer here.

That's it, baker. Ezra says God gave them “…new life to rebuild the house of our God and repair its ruins…” (Ezra 9:9). Rebuilding is work, and it's a gift too. They get to put the house of God back together.

Visiting a ruin is a pretty sad field trip, friend. Ezra says God gave them “…new life to rebuild the house of our God and repair its ruins…” (Ezra 9:9). They're not just looking at it. They're getting new life to fix it.
Guarding a pile of ruins is a job with no upside, baker. Ezra says the new life is “…to rebuild the house of our God and repair its ruins…” (Ezra 9:9). The word is rebuild. The ruins get repaired.

Yes, baker. The commandment Ezra quotes says, “…do not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters for your sons.” (Ezra 9:12). It goes both directions. Ezra says God gave this through His servants the prophets.

Servants aren't in this commandment, friend. Ezra quotes it this way: “…do not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters for your sons.” (Ezra 9:12). It's about daughters and sons.
Widows aren't mentioned in this one, baker. The quote says, “…do not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters for your sons.” (Ezra 9:12). The word is daughters.

It says the opposite, friend. The commandment Ezra quotes says, “Never seek their peace or prosperity…” (Ezra 9:12). So it doesn't tell Israel to seek it. Ezra is reading the commandment as God gave it through the prophets.
False is right, baker. The commandment Ezra quotes says, “Never seek their peace or prosperity…” (Ezra 9:12). That's what it says, plain as that. Ezra is repeating what God gave through the prophets.

explanations.answer: So they could be strong and pass the land on
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The commandment says, “…so that you may be strong and may eat the good things of the land, leaving it as an inheritance to your sons forever.” (Ezra 9:12). Strength and an inheritance for their sons are the reasons it gives.

explanations.answer: So they could pay less to foreign kings
explanations.explanation: Money doesn't come up in that commandment, friend. It says, “…so that you may be strong and may eat the good things of the land, leaving it as an inheritance to your sons forever.” (Ezra 9:12). The reasons are strength and an inheritance.

explanations.answer: So they could rule over every nation
explanations.explanation: Ruling the world is a big dream, baker, but that's not in the text. The commandment says, “…so that you may be strong and may eat the good things of the land, leaving it as an inheritance to your sons forever.” (Ezra 9:12). It's about strength and passing the land to their sons.
Other way around, friend. Ezra says, “…You, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserve…” (Ezra 9:13). He's not complaining that it was too much. He's admitting God held back.

False is right, baker. Ezra says “…You, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserve and have given us such a remnant as this…” (Ezra 9:13). Less than deserved, and a remnant on top of it.

explanations.answer: Wipe them out with no survivor
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Ezra asks, “Would You not become so angry with us as to wipe us out, leaving no remnant or survivor?” (Ezra 9:14). Notice it's a question he's asking. The text doesn't answer it in this prayer.

explanations.answer: Send them back down to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't part of this question, friend. Ezra asks, “Would You not become so angry with us as to wipe us out, leaving no remnant or survivor?” (Ezra 9:14). No remnant or survivor is the fear he names.

explanations.answer: Give their land over to Moab
explanations.explanation: Moab shows up in the leaders' list (Ezra 9:1), baker, but not in this question. Ezra asks, “Would You not become so angry with us as to wipe us out, leaving no remnant or survivor?” (Ezra 9:14). That's the weight of what he's asking.
That's it, baker. Ezra prays, “O LORD, God of Israel, You are righteous!” (Ezra 9:15). After all that confessing, this is where he lands. He doesn't argue his case, he just says who God is.
Ezra's talking like someone who's right there, friend. He's on his knees with his hands spread out to the LORD (Ezra 9:5). And the word he lands on is “…You are righteous!” (Ezra 9:15). Not distant.
In this scene, baker, it's Ezra doing the talking. He ends his prayer with “O LORD, God of Israel, You are righteous!” (Ezra 9:15). The word he uses for God is righteous.

True, baker. Ezra says, “Here we are before You in our guilt, though because of it no one can stand before You.” (Ezra 9:15). He doesn't dress it up. That's a heavy way to end a prayer, so I'll let it sit.

Ezra says it right at the end, friend. His words are, “Here we are before You in our guilt, though because of it no one can stand before You.” (Ezra 9:15). He says it plainly, with no excuses attached.
